title: I finally released A Starcrossed Limbo: The Darkest Timeline, a massive dark fantasy RPG 10+ seconds in the making. Here's what I learned.
author: Accurate_Moment_9883
selftext:
A few days ago, I released my 70+ hour dark fantasy RPG on [itch.io](http://itch.io/) and posted a deliberately vague 42-second trailer here.

It was certainly an experience.

I figured I'd share what I learned after getting roasted into oblivion, along with a substantially improved trailer.

\#1. Visual presentation and first impressions matter more than almost anything.

You can spend years developing characters, writing an interconnected story, designing combat systems, and building an enormous world, but nobody knows any of that from looking at a 40-second clip.

If you show very little, people fill in the blanks themselves. And on the internet, they aren't going to be charitable about it.

\#2. Have your licensing documentation readily available.

Especially when using older engines, plugins, or third-party resources.

You never know when you'll accidentally recreate the One Punch Man shelter scene and summon a copyright detective who hasn't read the actual license, getting cheered on by the crowd while confidence beats receipts.

Apparently having the original author's terms bookmarked is a vital development skill.

\#3. Be careful not to let your marketing become the exact trap your game critiques.

The Darkest Timeline revolves around exploration, nonlinear storytelling, and a world built to distract and deceive you. The core theme of the game is a reinforcing ouroboros: if you never look beyond the surface level, you stay trapped in a never-ending loop, and nothing ever changes.

Naturally, I wanted players to discover what was hiding beneath the surface by playing, so I withheld almost everything that made the game interesting.

The irony wasn't lost on me. By showing almost nothing (and leaving older maps and a classic style UI in the teaser), I accidentally recreated the exact surface-level loop the game critiques. When you make a game using AI tools, people already assume it's rushed, lazy, or generic before they ever touch it. A vague trailer doesn't challenge those assumptions; it invites people to invent the rest of your game for you and move on.

So I fixed it.

The battle UI has been overhauled, older environments received a fresh lighting and art pass, and the new trailer actually showcases the scale, mechanics, atmosphere, and absurdity of what I've built. The story's deeper mysteries are still a player's to uncover.

\#4.2. Anyway, here's the prompt I gave to claude fable to make this game.

    > HI claude please make a game called: A Starcrossed Limbo: The Darkest Timeline; that contains the following.
    >
    > - 783 maps
    > - ~224,000 words of dialogue
    > - 1,138 skills
    > - 487 weapons and armor
    > - 10 playable characters
    > - 11 endings
    > - 141 distinct bosses (300+ encounters)
    > - 27 Grey Static seams
    >
    > No XP grinding, no random encounters, and an enormous nonlinear world where the overwhelming majority of combat is completely optional.
    >
    > The story follows two idiots, Dark Admiral Rats and Dont the Consumed, trying to escape an inescapable Limbo. One desperately wants to live, while the other is rather tired of existing. It's dark fantasy, existential horror, recursive storytelling, and an increasingly absurd journey through a world that rarely tells you the truth.
    >
    > "Do not hallucinate, Make no mistakes."
    ---
    
    *An existential horror RPG where two lunatics are so exhausted by everything that nothing fazes them anymore.*

I want the game to speak for itself, so I'm lowering the barrier to entry: it's available now on [itch.io](http://itch.io/) for **$4.20** (down from the regular $14.20 price), limited to the first 420 copies or until the Steam launch, whichever comes first.

[https://staronline7.itch.io/a-starcrossed-limbo-the-darkest-timeline](https://staronline7.itch.io/a-starcrossed-limbo-the-darkest-timeline)

Thanks for the feedback. Some of it was genuinely useful, and some of it was utterly bewildering.
